name: api-gateway
context: Distributed systems requiring a single entry point for client requests to backend microservices, handling cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and routing.
benefits: Single entry point for clients, simplifying client code and endpoint management
Centralized cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting, logging, TLS termination)
Service discovery abstraction: clients don't need to know internal service locations
Protocol translation: clients use simpler protocols, gateway bridges to internal services
Reduced client code: gateway handles aggregation and transformation
Unified security policy: consistent authentication/authorization across all services
Centralized observability with unified access logs and metrics
tradeoffs: Single point of failure if not deployed with high availability
Additional latency (5-30ms per request depending on plugins and implementation)
Gateway becomes critical infrastructure requiring dedicated monitoring and on-call
Can become a performance bottleneck under heavy load without proper scaling
Introduces operational complexity: another system to deploy, configure, and maintain
Risk of becoming a mega-service if overloaded with business logic
use_cases: Multiple clients consuming the same backend services
Mobile and web clients with different data needs (use BFF pattern)
Public APIs requiring rate limiting, authentication, and quota management
Need unified monitoring and centralized access logging
Migrating from monolith to microservices using strangler fig pattern
Protocol translation between client-facing APIs and internal services
avoid_when: Single client with direct service access (adds unnecessary complexity)
Small teams without capacity to operate critical infrastructure
Strong consistency requirements where every millisecond counts
Services are tightly coupled and must be deployed together anyway
component_types: API Gateway: Single entry point handling routing, authentication, rate limiting (Kong, Envoy, AWS API Gateway, Apigee, NGINX)
Service Registry/Discovery: Maintains service endpoint locations and health status (Consul, Eureka)
Backend for Frontend (BFF): Per-client-type gateway for client-specific data needs and aggregation
Load Balancer: Distributes traffic across multiple gateway instances for high availability
Cache Store: Stores rate limiting counters, JWKS keys, and response caches (Redis)
Observability Stack: Collects metrics, logs, and traces (OpenTelemetry collector, Prometheus)
Request Router: Maps incoming requests to appropriate backend services based on path, headers, method
Authentication Handler: Validates JWT tokens, API keys, OAuth tokens centrally
Rate Limiter: Enforces per-client or per-endpoint rate limits using token bucket or sliding window
Response Aggregator: Combines data from multiple services into unified response
technology_stack: Kong (Lua/OpenResty, declarative config, rich plugin ecosystem)
Envoy (C++ proxy, xDS dynamic configuration, native OTel)
AWS API Gateway (fully managed, integrates with AWS Lambda)
Redis (rate limiting counters, JWKS caching, response caching)
anti_patterns: Smart Gateway: putting business logic (if/else on request body content) in the gateway
Distributed Monolith: gateway that requires coordinated deployment with all services
Gateway Per Team: separate gateways per team causing inconsistent auth/rate limiting
Over-aggregation: gateway that fans out to too many services creating tight coupling
No Circuit Breaker: slow services blocking gateway threads
Missing Observability: not tracking gateway latency (p50/p99), error rate separately
Monolithic Gateway Config: one giant gateway handling everything instead of BFF split
design_principles: Single Responsibility: Gateway handles cross-cutting concerns only; business logic belongs in services
Keep It Thin: Authentication, rate limiting, routing, observability — no business logic
Validate JWTs Once: Pass verified identity downstream via headers; services trust gateway authentication
Design for Failure: Implement circuit breakers, timeouts, and fallbacks; deploy in active-active clusters
High Availability: Deploy multiple gateway instances with health checks and auto-scaling
Observability First: Instrument with OpenTelemetry from day one; track gateway latency separately from backend
Stateless Configuration: Store gateway config in version control; use declarative configuration
Security by Default: Enable authentication, rate limiting, and TLS from day one
best_practices: Keep the gateway thin: Handle only cross-cutting concerns. Business logic belongs in services, not the gateway
Design for failure: Implement circuit breakers, timeouts, and fallbacks. Deploy in active-active clusters
Secure by default: Enable authentication, rate limiting, and TLS from day one
Cache strategically: Cache responses at the gateway level for read-heavy, public data
Monitor gateway latency separately: Track p50/p99 latency added by gateway independently from backend services
Use OpenTelemetry: OpenTelemetry compliance critical for observability and distributed tracing
Start simple: Basic routing and authentication first, add features as needs grow
Validate JWTs once: Pass identity downstream via headers; services trust gateway
Deploy in clusters: Multiple gateway instances prevent single point of failure
Implement dynamic throttling: Adjust rate limits based on traffic volume and user trust
